issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff in a possession suit may plead a primary claim that the occupant is a gratuitous licensee and an alternative claim for eviction on tenancy-related grounds, even if the claims are inconsistent.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that the occupants held the premises under a gratuitous licence and that the licence had been terminated.
The occupants denied being licensees and asserted that they occupied the premises as tenants, while admitting that the property belonged to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff alternatively sought possession on grounds available under rent-control law.
The tenancy and licence claims were put in issue and tried, and the trial court considered the alternative grounds without the occupants being taken by surprise.
The first appellate court granted possession on the primary licence claim, finding that the occupants were licensees whose licence had been validly terminated.
issues.conclusion: The alternative tenancy-based plea was not barred merely because it was inconsistent with the primary licence claim. In any event, the alternative plea did not undermine relief granted on the primary claim.
issues.legal_principle: There is no absolute bar on pleading inconsistent claims or defences in the alternative. Under Srinivas Ram Kumar v. Mahabir Prasad (AIR 1951 SC 177), inconsistent claims may be pleaded in the alternative. Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul (AIR 1966 SC 735) recognises that, where the competing pleaded relationships are tenancy and licence, the evidence may establish one even if the other is not proved. G. Nagamma v. Siromenamma ((1996) 2 SCC 25) and B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai (2000 (1) SCC 712) affirm that inconsistent alternative pleas are generally permissible, subject to the restriction against an amendment that deprives the opposing party of the benefit of an earlier admission. Under J.J. Lal Pvt. Ltd. v. M.R. Murali ((2002) 3 SCC 98), an alternative relief based on the opponent’s pleaded facts may be granted where those facts expressly admit entitlement to that relief, the opponent is not taken by surprise, no injustice results, and the interests of justice do not require a separate suit. The alternative plea need not be considered when relief is granted on the primary claim.

rule.if: possession_suit and primary_license_claim_pleaded and alternative_tenancy_relief_pleaded and defendant_admitted_ownership_and_tenant_occupation and alternative_issue_fully_tried and defendant_not_surprised and no_injustice_from_alternative_plea and alternative_relief_could_be_sought_separately

predicates.possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession of occupied premises.
predicates.primary_license_claim_pleaded: The plaintiff alleged that the occupants held the premises under a gratuitous licence that had been terminated.
predicates.alternative_tenancy_relief_pleaded: The plaintiff also sought eviction on grounds applicable if the occupants were tenants.
predicates.defendant_admitted_ownership_and_tenant_: The occupants stated that they occupied the premises as tenants and admitted that the property belonged to the plaintiff.
predicates.alternative_issue_fully_tried: The parties had the opportunity to present evidence on the alternative tenancy-related issue, and the court considered it.
predicates.defendant_not_surprised: The occupants had notice of the alternative claim and were not taken by surprise by its trial.
predicates.no_injustice_from_alternative_plea: Trying the alternative claim did not cause injustice to the occupants.
predicates.alternative_relief_could_be_sought_separ: The plaintiff could have sought the same alternative relief in a separate suit.

issues.definition: When the stated possession-suit, pleading, admission, and fairness predicates are present, the inconsistent alternative plea is permissible.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court in a second appeal cannot set aside a first appellate court’s evidence-based finding that occupants were licensees solely because the plaintiff also pleaded an inconsistent alternative tenancy claim.
material_facts: The first appellate court reappraised the evidence and found that the occupants and their predecessor had occupied the premises as gratuitous licensees.
The absence of a rent note or other evidence of rent supported the first appellate court’s finding that there was no tenancy.
The first appellate court found that the licence had been validly terminated.
The High Court did not reject those factual findings on their merits; it dismissed the suit because it considered the alternative tenancy plea contradictory to the licence claim.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s approach was improper. Its judgment was set aside and the first appellate court’s judgment and decree were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the relationship established by the evidence is that of licensor and licensee or landlord and tenant is a question of fact to be determined from the totality of the evidence. The High Court could not displace the first appellate court’s finding on that question merely because the plaintiff had also pleaded an alternative tenancy-based claim; the alternative claim did not affect the decree granted on the primary licence case.

predicates.civil_second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court was a second appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_license_on_e: The first appellate court assessed the evidence and found that the occupants held the premises under a licence rather than a tenancy.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_licence_vali: The first appellate court found that the licence had been validly terminated.
predicates.high_court_left_factual_findings_undistu: The High Court did not set aside the first appellate court’s factual findings on their evidentiary merits.
predicates.high_court_reversed_only_because_alterna: The High Court reversed the result solely because it regarded the alternative tenancy plea as contradictory to the primary licence plea.

issues.definition: When these predicates describe a second appeal, the High Court’s reversal based only on inconsistent alternative pleading is unsustainable.
